strengths: The paper targets a real and timely gap: evaluating mobile GUI agents that combine ordinary UI actions with shortcuts such as APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts. This is relevant to current NLP/agent evaluation work and the benchmark framing is useful.

MAS-Bench has a reasonably concrete scope: 139 tasks across 11 real-world Android applications, with single-app and cross-app tasks, predefined shortcuts, and metrics covering success, time, steps, token cost, shortcut usage, and shortcut success.

The experiments compare GUI-only agents with shortcut-augmented variants across different perceptual modalities, and the reported improvements are directionally plausible: predefined shortcuts improve success and efficiency, especially for weaker base models and longer cross-app tasks.

The paper also attempts to evaluate shortcut generation, not just shortcut use. The finding that generated shortcuts are less robust than hand-crafted predefined shortcuts is useful and appropriately highlights an open research problem.
The appendix provides some helpful environment details, action-space definitions, task/app breakdowns, and failure-case analysis, which makes the benchmark more interpretable.
weaknesses: The reproducibility story is not yet strong enough for a clear positive recommendation. Critical details are missing or underspecified, including exact app versions, emulator state initialization, account/data setup, full task list, shortcut implementations, automated evaluators, prompts, retry policies, and whether all code/knowledge bases will be released.

The success evaluation is vague. The paper says it adapts SPA-Bench and embeds shortcut action descriptions to determine success/failure, but it does not sufficiently specify goal-state checks, evaluator reliability, false-positive/false-negative rates, or manual validation. This is especially important because benchmark claims hinge on automated success labels.

The benchmark design may be partially circular: every task is constructed to have one or more invocable predefined shortcuts, and the shortcut knowledge base is hand curated. This demonstrates that shortcuts can help, but it weakens claims about general GUI-shortcut agent capability in less engineered environments.

The shortcut-generation evaluation has possible leakage and fairness concerns. Generated shortcuts are built from trajectories on benchmark tasks and then evaluated on a 50% random task subset; the paper does not clearly separate generation tasks from evaluation tasks or explain how repeated subtask overlap is controlled.

Baselines and statistical rigor are limited. Results appear to be single-run measurements with no confidence intervals, variance estimates, significance tests, or robustness checks across app versions, UI changes, accounts, or devices. Given the stochasticity of LLM agents and mobile environments, this limits confidence in the magnitude of the reported gains.

Several metrics are confusing or insufficiently motivated. For example, GSAR is described as a GUI-to-shortcut action ratio where a high ratio is said to indicate efficient shortcut use, which seems counterintuitive without more explanation. MSRS and human-step normalization also need clearer definitions and edge-case handling.

The comparison to prior benchmarks and the claim of being the first benchmark for this setting are plausible but somewhat overstated. Related work on API/GUI agents, mobile automation, and self-improving agents is discussed, but the novelty boundary relative to AndroidWorld, SPA-Bench, MobileAgent-E, AppAgentX, and API-GUI hybrid evaluations could be sharper.

The paper contains presentation issues that reduce clarity: formatting artifacts, missing or incomplete project-page information, inconsistent naming, occasional grammar problems, and some tables whose columns are hard to parse from the manuscript.

The contribution is more of a promising benchmark proposal than a fully convincing, reusable evaluation standard at this stage. With stronger release details, evaluator validation, leakage controls, and robustness analysis, it could become a solid Findings paper.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant gap: evaluating mobile GUI agents that combine ordinary GUI actions with shortcuts such as APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts. This is a useful direction for NLP/agent research because efficiency and robustness are increasingly important for long-horizon GUI agents.

MAS-Bench has a concrete benchmark design with 139 tasks across 11 Android apps, a taxonomy of shortcut types, and multiple evaluation dimensions covering task success, efficiency, token cost, shortcut calls, and shortcut success.

The experiments compare several agent families and input modalities, including GUI-only baselines and shortcut-augmented variants, and the reported results consistently suggest that well-designed predefined shortcuts can improve success rate and efficiency.
The paper includes some useful diagnostic analysis of failure modes, such as shortcut selection/planning errors and failure to switch back from shortcuts to GUI actions.
weaknesses: The central claims are overstated relative to the evidence. Claims such as being the first systematic benchmark, framework-agnostic effectiveness, and successful evaluation of shortcut generation are supported only by a small set of agents, one main model family, and limited analysis.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The abstract says the project page is available but no URL appears in the extracted manuscript; the full task list, app versions, shortcut definitions, prompts, evaluation scripts, random seeds, and environment reset procedures are not sufficiently specified.

The benchmark construction risks circularity: every task is designed to have one or more invocable predefined shortcuts from the authors’ knowledge base, and the predefined shortcuts are manually curated for the same benchmark. This makes the gains from MAS agents less surprising and may not reflect discovery or generalization to unseen apps/tasks.

The automated success evaluation is vague. The paper says it adapts SPA-Bench and embeds shortcut action descriptions to determine success/failure, but does not provide enough detail or validation against human judgments to establish reliability.

The shortcut generation evaluation is weak. Generated shortcuts are evaluated on a 50% random task subset, but the split protocol, whether shortcut generation and evaluation are separated cleanly, and whether generated shortcuts overfit task histories are unclear. The reported generated shortcuts often underperform the baseline, yet the paper still frames this as validating the benchmark.

Several metrics are underdefined or inconsistently motivated. For example, the “optimal” step count for MSR is not clearly derived, GSAR is described in a way that is hard to interpret, and execution time can be confounded by emulator/app/network variability.

The experimental analysis lacks statistical testing, confidence intervals, repeated runs, or robustness checks across app states and versions. Given the small task count and dynamic mobile environment, this limits confidence in the reported improvements.

The comparison to prior benchmarks is too coarse and largely checklist-based. It does not deeply analyze overlap with AndroidWorld, SPA-Bench, MobileAgent-E-style shortcuts, or API/GUI hybrid agent evaluations.

Writing and presentation issues reduce clarity: there are grammatical errors, missing details, inconsistent terminology, and some appendix references do not appear to contain the promised information, such as the detailed task list.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and underexplored evaluation problem: mobile GUI agents that can combine GUI actions with shortcuts such as APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts. This is relevant to current NLP/agent work and the benchmark framing is clear.

MAS-Bench is concrete and reasonably scoped, with 139 tasks across 11 real-world Android apps, 88 predefined shortcuts, multiple task types, and metrics covering success, execution efficiency, token cost, shortcut use, and shortcut reliability.

The experimental results support the main qualitative claim that shortcut-augmented agents can improve both success rate and efficiency over GUI-only baselines, especially for weaker models and cross-app tasks.

The paper goes beyond predefined shortcut use by proposing an evaluation protocol for agent-generated shortcuts, revealing useful negative/diagnostic findings: replay shortcuts are brittle, dynamic shortcuts remain imperfect, and predefined shortcuts are substantially more robust.
The benchmark includes several relevant baselines with different observation modalities, which helps show that the shortcut mechanism is not tied to a single agent architecture.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is under-specified. The abstract says a project page is available, but the URL appears blank in the manuscript; it is unclear whether the emulator setup, app versions/APKs, task definitions, shortcut knowledge base, evaluators, and prompts will be fully released.

The task and shortcut construction may bake in strong benchmark-specific assumptions. Every task is designed to have useful shortcuts from the curated knowledge base, so the measured gains may partly reflect benchmark design rather than general shortcut discovery or real-world applicability.

The automated success evaluation is not described rigorously enough. The paper says it adapts SPA-Bench and embeds shortcut action descriptions to determine success, but does not give enough detail on validation, false positive/negative rates, or how task-specific end states are checked.

Experimental rigor is limited by missing variance estimates, statistical testing, repeated runs, and seed/control details. Since GUI-agent performance is stochastic and environment-sensitive, single aggregate scores may overstate the robustness of the conclusions.

The shortcut-generation evaluation is interesting but not fully convincing as an evaluation of autonomous generation. Shortcuts are generated from M3A histories using Gemini-2.5-Pro and then tested through T3A, but the split protocol, leakage risks, task overlap, and fairness of comparing hand-crafted versus generated shortcuts need sharper treatment.

Some claims are too strong or imprecise, including “first benchmark” and “fair, reproducible, and in-depth assessment,” given related mobile-agent benchmarks and the current lack of release/evaluator detail.

The paper would benefit from deeper analysis of shortcut failures, app-version brittleness, security/privacy implications of API/deep-link/RPA access, and how much manual engineering is needed to maintain shortcuts across real applications.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and relevant gap: evaluation of mobile agents that mix GUI interaction with APIs, deep links, and RPA-style shortcuts. This is a useful extension beyond GUI-only mobile-agent benchmarks.

MAS-Bench is reasonably broad for a new benchmark, with 139 tasks across 11 real applications, both single-app and cross-app workflows, 88 predefined shortcuts, difficulty levels, human GUI step baselines, and metrics covering success, efficiency, cost, shortcut use, and shortcut reliability.

The experimental coverage is strong: the paper evaluates multiple agentic workflows, general-purpose VLMs, and specialized GUI models, with paired GUI-only versus shortcut-augmented comparisons. The results convincingly show that well-chosen shortcuts can improve success and efficiency, while poor shortcut selection can hurt performance.

The paper includes valuable diagnostic analyses beyond headline success rates, including shortcut precision/recall, redundancy, irrelevant-shortcut interference, task difficulty breakdowns, generated-shortcut variants, and failure-case analysis.
The automated evaluation pipeline is at least partially validated against human labels on 278 trajectories, with high reported agreement, which supports scalability of the benchmark evaluation.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is not yet fully convincing. The benchmark depends on live Android apps, test accounts, app versions, emulator snapshots, collected shortcuts, RPA scripts, and an LLM-based evaluator. The paper describes these components, but does not provide enough concrete release detail to know whether external users can recreate the exact environment; the project page appears blank in the manuscript text.

The predefined shortcut knowledge base is partly handcrafted and may encode substantial task-specific knowledge. Because every task has one or more usable predefined shortcuts, the reported gains may partly reflect benchmark/shortcut co-design rather than general shortcut discovery or robust hybrid-agent capability.

The shortcut-generation evaluation is relatively weak compared with the predefined-shortcut evaluation. It uses a 50% subset of the same benchmark, several generated shortcut sets have low success or reduced task success, and it is not fully clear how leakage between generation trajectories and evaluation tasks is prevented. The evidence supports the framework as diagnostic, but not strong progress on generation itself.

The automated judge validation is limited: it is evaluated on trajectories from MAS-MobileAgent only, and the judge uses Gemini models that are also used in some agent baselines. More diverse validation across agents, apps, and failure modes would better establish that success rates are not judge- or model-family biased.

Some claims are overstated. Terms such as “first,” “unified,” and “comprehensive” are plausible but not fully established against closely related GUI/API hybrid or mobile automation work. The paper would benefit from a sharper distinction between the benchmark contribution and the proposed MAS shortcut-injection baselines.

The benchmark scale is useful but still modest: 139 tasks, 11 apps, 7 RPA scripts, and one standardized emulator configuration. Generalization to app updates, real devices, different regions/accounts, and larger noisier shortcut pools remains mostly argued rather than demonstrated.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and timely gap: evaluating mobile GUI agents that can combine ordinary GUI actions with APIs, deep links, and RPA-style shortcuts. This is a meaningful direction for agent evaluation, especially because efficiency and shortcut misuse are not well captured by standard GUI-only benchmarks.

MAS-Bench includes a concrete dynamic Android environment, 139 tasks across 11 real applications, a curated shortcut knowledge base, multiple agent families, and several efficiency/cost metrics. The breadth of baselines is a real positive, and the results do show that access to reliable shortcuts can improve success rate and reduce execution cost for some agents.

The paper usefully separates predefined-shortcut use from shortcut-generation evaluation. The finding that generated shortcuts are much less robust than curated shortcuts is plausible and informative.

The authors provide some important reproducibility details, including emulator configuration, snapshot reset, test-account isolation, action space, human GUI baselines, and validation of the automated evaluator against human judgments.
weaknesses: The main empirical claim is partly built into the benchmark design: every task is constructed to have one or more invocable predefined shortcuts, and the shortcut inventory is curated by the authors. Showing that agents improve when given reliable, task-relevant shortcuts is useful, but less surprising and less conclusive than the paper’s framing suggests.

Reproducibility remains under-specified for a benchmark paper. The extracted manuscript does not provide a concrete project URL, full task list, shortcut definitions, app versions/APKs, prompts, evaluation scripts, or release plan sufficient to independently reproduce the results. This is a major concern because the benchmark depends heavily on dynamic apps, account state, Android intents, and curated deep links.

The automated evaluator is promising but not fully convincing. It is validated on 278 trajectories from MAS-MobileAgent, but the evaluation results in the paper cover many different agent types and failure modes. There is no clear evidence that the judge is equally reliable across all models, generated-shortcut failures, irrelevant-shortcut settings, or tasks where final state is subtle.

The experimental methodology lacks uncertainty estimates and robustness analysis. Results appear to be single-run averages over a relatively small benchmark, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance over seeds/model stochasticity. Several claims of substantial improvement would be more convincing with repeated trials.

The shortcut generation evaluation is relatively weak. It uses only a 50% subset of tasks, the generated shortcuts are produced through specific hand-designed strategies and Gemini/M3A pipelines, and the evaluation mainly shows that current generated shortcuts underperform curated ones. This supports MAS-Bench as a diagnostic tool only partially, not yet as a strong benchmark for autonomous shortcut discovery.

The paper sometimes overstates novelty and generality. Claims such as being the first unified benchmark and establishing framework-agnostic effectiveness are not fully justified, especially given the small set of apps, curated shortcuts, emulator-only setting, and mixed results where some augmented models do not improve or misuse shortcuts.

Some baselines and metrics are unevenly reported. Token costs are missing for many Agent-as-a-Model and specialized GUI model rows, and the comparison between GUI-only agents, prompted shortcut variants, and workflow agents may conflate base-model capability, prompt design, action-space design, and shortcut quality.

The benchmark’s external validity is uncertain. The tasks are only 139 examples, many are incremental variations, and evaluation is limited to standardized emulators rather than real devices or naturally changing app states. The claimed stability of shortcuts across app versions is encouraging but insufficiently documented for independent verification.

strengths: The paper targets a timely and under-benchmarked problem: evaluating mobile agents that combine GUI interaction with shortcuts such as APIs, deep links, and RPA scripts. This is relevant to current NLP/agent research and the benchmark fills a plausible gap beyond GUI-only mobile benchmarks.

MAS-Bench is reasonably well specified: 139 tasks across 11 real Android apps, 88 predefined shortcuts, single-app and cross-app tasks, difficulty levels, human GUI baselines, and multiple efficiency/cost metrics. The task design explicitly requires hybrid GUI-shortcut use rather than allowing shortcuts to trivially solve whole tasks.

The experimental coverage is broad. The paper evaluates agentic workflows, general-purpose VLMs, specialized GUI models, and shortcut-augmented variants, showing consistent gains for many models and also documenting failures where shortcut use hurts weaker or poorly adapted agents.

The paper goes beyond success rate by analyzing step efficiency, execution time, token cost, shortcut recall/precision, redundancy, no-relevant-shortcut interference, difficulty levels, and base-model capability. This makes the central claim more convincing than a simple benchmark leaderboard.

The shortcut-generation evaluation is a useful addition. Comparing predefined shortcuts, replay-style shortcuts, dynamic shortcuts, and MobileAgent-E-generated shortcuts under a common executor provides evidence that the benchmark can expose shortcut robustness and quality gaps.

The authors make a serious attempt to validate automated evaluation, reporting comparison against 278 human-annotated trajectories with high F1/precision/recall, which supports scalability of the benchmark evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: Reproducibility remains the main concern. The benchmark depends on live Android apps, dedicated accounts, app versions, emulator snapshots, deep links, and shortcut implementations, but the manuscript does not clearly state what will be released or provide a usable project link. Without the AVD images, accounts, scripts, shortcut database, task definitions, and evaluator prompts, independent reproduction would be difficult.

The benchmark size is modest for a main-conference benchmark claim: 139 tasks over 11 apps, with only 47 cross-app tasks and a 69-task subset for shortcut-generation evaluation. This is valuable but still somewhat small relative to the breadth of claims about hybrid mobile agents.

The predefined shortcut knowledge base is manually curated and intentionally aligned with the task set. This makes the benchmark useful for controlled evaluation, but it may overstate real-world shortcut availability and does not fully test open-ended shortcut discovery or retrieval in large/noisy shortcut spaces.

The comparison between predefined and agent-generated shortcuts is informative but not fully conclusive. The generated shortcut methods are relatively simple or adapted from existing agents, and the random 50% subset protocol is not described with enough detail to assess variance, sensitivity to task split, or statistical reliability.

The automated judge validation is encouraging, but it is based on trajectories from MAS-MobileAgent only. It is unclear whether judge reliability holds equally for very different agents, failure modes, shortcut types, and apps, especially when subtle task constraints or side effects are involved.

Several reported gains are heterogeneous: some specialized GUI models do not benefit, Qwen3-VL-4B can become less efficient, and ScaleCUA variants barely invoke shortcuts. The paper discusses these cases, but they temper the generality of the claim that shortcut augmentation broadly improves agents.

The paper would benefit from stronger statistical treatment, such as repeated runs, confidence intervals, significance testing, and sensitivity to app state drift. Dynamic GUI-agent benchmarks can have high variance, and single aggregate scores may hide instability.

Some methodological details are still high level, including shortcut retrieval prompts, action-space mapping, generated-shortcut construction prompts, exact app versions, and evaluator prompts. These details matter because small prompt or environment differences can materially affect agent performance.
